assumptions: The feature flag is treated as the cause on the strength of timing and error-type correlation only. No rollback or disable was attempted, so the hypothesis was never verified by observing recovery.

The alert's end timestamp coincides exactly with the moment the automated responder escalated, not with any observed return to normal. Recovery is assumed, not evidenced; the newest log line available still shows the elevated error rate with the flag fully on.
Impact is assumed to be confined to account page rendering, because that is the only request type appearing in the logs reviewed. Whether other surfaces evaluate the same flag was not checked.
The underlying defect (what the new code path divides by) was never located in source; it is inferred entirely from the exception type in the logs.

No deploy or change record exists in the 24h lookback, so the flag flip is assumed to have been a runtime configuration change rather than a code release. The person or system that flipped it is unknown.
Request volume is assumed steady, based on the flag-evaluation lines consistently reporting 200 evaluations per minute.
The log excerpt covering 15:14-15:23 appears three times in the investigation record; this is assumed to be repeated reads of the same window rather than distinct events.
input.executive_summary: On 12 September 2026, a new spending-summary feature was switched on for the shop's customer account page. The code behind that feature failed when it tried to render the page, so customers loading their account page began seeing errors instead. Failures started when the feature was first shown to a small slice of traffic at 15:18 UTC and became widespread one minute later when it was switched on for everyone. The automated responder opened an incident at 15:24 UTC, correctly identified the newly enabled feature as the cause within about twenty seconds, and re-confirmed that conclusion twice more. However, it was not permitted to take any corrective action on its own, so it made no change to the service and handed the incident to a human engineer at 15:26 UTC. Nothing in the record shows the feature being switched back off or the account page recovering: the last available data still shows failures at roughly the same elevated level, so customer impact should be assumed to have continued past the point where the alert closed until a person intervened. Other pages and functions were not implicated. A low, pre-existing level of payment-authorisation timeouts was present before, during and after the event and was not part of this incident.
input.root_cause: Enabling the `monthly-spend-feature` flag on io-shop exposed a code path that raises ZeroDivisionError while rendering the account page; the flag went from off to a 4/200 canary at 15:18 and to 100% at 15:19, and the account-page error rate stepped from a ~1-2% UpstreamTimeout baseline to the high-twenties/thirties in the same minute, with the excess errors being ZeroDivisionError. This is a correlation-based conclusion: no rollback or other action was taken, so the causal link was never confirmed by test.
